query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Post-deposition annealing that promotes microstructural homogenization and grain refinement in FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings will enhance high‐temperature sliding wear resistance by limiting dislocation mobility and reducing localized plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate, with a relatively inhomogeneous microstructure and residual stress from processing.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment (e.g., at approximately 700 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere) to promote microstructural homogenization and grain refinement.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests conducted within the intended operating regime (approximately 500–700 °C) under similar load and sliding speeds.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, more uniform solid solution microstructure with reduced residual stresses and smaller grain sizes.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment reduces microstructural heterogeneities and residual stresses, thereby hindering dislocation mobility and suppressing dynamic recrystallization during sliding. This leads to a more uniform stress distribution and limits localized plastic deformation that would otherwise accelerate wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed coating will exhibit increased hardness, a lower wear rate, and reduced evidence of microscopic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating without post-deposition annealing.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in high-temperature regimes (approximately 500–700 °C) where thermally activated deformation mechanisms dominate; results at lower temperatures may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and time may require further tuning, and the potential for oxidation (if not fully controlled) could alter the microstructure and surface chemistry, affecting wear behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FeNiCrCoCu coated samples on a conventional metal substrate. Subject one set to the controlled annealing treatment (700 °C, 1 hour, inert atmosphere) while keeping the other set as-deposited. Conduct identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (at ~600 °C, under controlled load and sliding speed) on both sample sets.
measurements: Microhardness of the coating (pre- and post-test)
Wear rate (mass loss or volume loss)
Grain size and residual stress analysis via microscopy and diffraction techniques
Surface morphology and evidence of plastic deformation (via SEM or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in hardness and wear resistance (i.e., lower wear rate and less pronounced microscopic plastic deformation) compared to the as-deposited baseline under high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis that annealing-induced microstructural refinement is the dominant mechanism governing wear resistance is falsified.

Structure and Wear Resistance of TiC-Reinforced Al1.8CrCuFeNi2 High-Entropy Alloy Coating Using Laser Cladding

Abstract: AbstractAl1.8CrCuFeNi2 high-entropy alloy coatings with different TiC contents were prepared using laser cladding. The effect of TiC on the microstructure, hardness and wear resistance of the coatings was investigated. It was found that the phase structure of the coating with 10 wt.% TiC was a single BCC phase with no other precipitated phase. When 20 wt.% TiC was added, the phase structure of the coating was a BCC phase and TiC phase. When the TiC content increased to 30 wt.%, more TiC-reinforcing phase was formed. With the increase in the TiC content, the hardness of the high-entropy alloy coating was enhanced and the wear loss clearly decreased, which was closely related to the change in the coating structure. Microstructure and Friction Properties of AlCrTiVNbx High-Entropy Alloys via Annealing Manufactured by Vacuum Arc Melting

Abstract: To enhance the friction and wear properties of alloys, AlCrTiVNbx high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with various Nb contents were prepared using the arc melting technique and then annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h. The microstructure and hardness changes in the AlCrTiVNbx (x = 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5) HEAs after casting and annealing were studied via scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffractometry, optical microscopy and the Vickers hardness test. The MFT-EC400 ball disc reciprocating friction and wear tester was used to investigate the wear resistance of the HEAs before and after annealing. The results show that the annealed AlCrTiVNbx HEAs changed from a single-phase structure to a multi-phase structure, and the content of the face-center cubic (FCC) phase and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase further increases with the increase in Nb content. The hardness value of the annealed HEAs is greatly enhanced compared with the casting state, and the hardness of the Nb0.5 HEA is increased from 543 HV to 725 HV after annealing.
